newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PEASANTS WANT 1998 BUDGET GAP TO STAY FLAT.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PEASANTS WANT 1998 BUDGET GAP TO STAY FLAT.

text.p: Poland's co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL) demanded on Friday that 1998 budget deficit remained at this year's levels and criticised the finance ministry's plan to slash it to cool buoyant domestic demand.
PSL, the smaller party in the government, said it wanted the 1998 budget gap to stay at 2.8 percent of gross domestic product rather that see it cut to 1.9 percent as the finance minister wants.

"The 1.9 percent (deficit) is an index which surely supports our Euroepan Union aspirations but it does not secure needs of the Polish citizens," Roman Jagielinski, senior Peasant official, told a news conference.
"We think we can stick at least to the (deficit) index planned for 1997," he said, adding his party wanted to secure higher spending on agriculture, investment and stimulation of exports.
Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Thursday he would ignore the Peasants' protests and continue working on the 1998 budget draft assuming that the deficit would be cut.
He earlier warned that a higher deficit would continue to fuel strong demand for imported goods and might push the swelling trade and current account deficits beyond control.

The central bank says that if the current account deficit, forecast to grow to $6 billion this year from $1.35 billion in 1996, expands too much in 1998 Poland might eventually have to devalue the zloty. It says this would boost inflation and undermine economic growth.

The bank advocates balancing the budget next year or at least cutting it to 1.5 percent of GDP before getting rid of deficit in 1999, the measure which would help Poland avoid a Czech-style financial crisis.
The Czech Republic had to devalue its currency and take strict anti-import measures after its foreign trade deficit ballooned and industrial output shrank.
PSL president Waldemar Pawlak agreed that the trade deficit growth had to be curbed but said this should involve stimulating exports rather than limiting imports by cooling internal demand.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz of the ex-communist party supports the finance ministry's austerity plans and his political allies in the government can overrule the Peasants objections at a cabinet vote on the budget draft.
Belka wants to finish his budget draft by early September so as the government could submit it shortly after the September 21 general elections, along with the resignation of the prime minister.
Under his proposal, next year's budgetary spending will be 142.9 billion zlotys, revenues 133.3 billion zlotys and deficit 9.6 billion zlotys.
Inflation is to fall to 9.5 percent in December next year from 14.6 percent in May while economic growth is forecast to continue at this year's rate of 5.5 percent. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
